title: Horse Racing Basics and Meeting the Data
sub: Taking on the "80% wall" with data science
goal: Explain how horse racing in Japan works, and race conditions and grades
Read a race card and say what information it contains
Explain how odds and popularity work, and the payout rate (the 80% wall)
Find the horse racing data on Kaggle and explore it

sec.h: What we will do in this course
p: Over 11 classes, we will analyze horse racing data. The goal is to think about how to grow virtual money in a reproducible way.
Horse racing mixes many factors: horses, jockeys, distance, weather, popularity and more. You cannot look at everything at once. That is why a point of view — where to look — matters.
With the right point of view, you can find clear, statistically meaningful differences even in complex data. Building that feeling is the aim of this course.
All money is virtual. We never actually bet. In Japan, the law says you must be 20 or older to buy betting tickets.

sec.h: How horse racing works in Japan
p: Japan has central racing, run by the JRA (Japan Racing Association), and local racing, run by local governments and others. Our data is from central racing.
Central racing takes place at 10 racecourses: Sapporo, Hakodate, Fukushima, Niigata, Tokyo, Nakayama, Chukyo, Kyoto, Hanshin and Kokura.
Races are mainly held on Saturdays and Sundays. Up to 18 horses can run in one race.
Courses are either turf (grass) or dirt (sand). Some horses are good on turf, others on dirt.
Distances range from about 1000m to 3600m. Some horses are good at short distances, others at long ones.
When rain makes the course wet, running changes. This is called track condition, in four levels: good (良), slightly heavy (稍重), heavy (重) and bad (不良).
Racecourses also differ: right- or left-handed, the length of the final straight, whether there is a hill, and so on.
Each time a horse wins, it moves up a class. It starts with newcomer races (新馬戦) and maiden races (未勝利戦), then 1-win class, 2-win class, 3-win class, and open class.
The highest open races are graded stakes: G3, G2 and G1, in rising order. G1 races include the Japanese Derby, the Japan Cup and the Arima Kinen.
Higher grades gather stronger horses. Whether results are more upset-prone by grade is one of the viewpoints we will investigate.
Class names changed in 2019. Before that, they were called 500万下, 1000万下 and 1600万下, which match today's 1-win, 2-win and 3-win classes. When using older data, you need to align the names.
Before a race, a race card (出馬表) is published. It lists the horses that will run.
It shows the bracket number (1–8) and horse number, the horse's name, sex and age, the weight carried (斤量, in kg), the jockey, body weight and its change from last time, last race result and more.
Each bracket has a color. From bracket 1: white, black, red, blue, yellow, green, orange, pink.
Odds are not decided by the organizer. They are decided by the share of money everyone bets. This is called the pari-mutuel system.
The less money bet on a horse to win, the higher its odds — what you get back if it wins.
But not all the money is paid back. For win bets, 80% goes to payouts and the other 20% is deducted.
Horses are called favorite #1, #2… from the lowest odds. Popularity is many people's prediction, not strength itself. Where people's predictions are biased, there is a chance for analysis.
Win (単勝): pick the winner (payout rate 80%)
Place (複勝): pick a horse that finishes in the top 3; top 2 if 7 or fewer horses run (80%)
Bracket quinella (枠連): the brackets of 1st and 2nd (77.5%)
Quinella (馬連): the horses that finish 1st and 2nd, in any order (77.5%)
Wide (ワイド): two horses that both finish in the top 3 (77.5%)
Exacta (馬単): 1st and 2nd in exact order (75%)
Trio (3連複): the top 3 horses in any order (75%)
Trifecta (3連単): the top 3 in exact order (72.5%)
So if you keep betting without thinking, on average your money shrinks to 80% or less. This is the "80% wall" we will take on in this course.

sec.h: Finding the horse racing data on Kaggle
p: Kaggle is a website where data scientists around the world share data and compete in analysis.
1. Create a Kaggle account (free)
2. Open the "JRA日本中央競馬会 Horse Racing Dataset" page (the link is under "Want to learn more?" below)
3. Read the data description (Data Card) and the column names. They are written in Japanese and English
4. In the "Code" tab, look at how other people have analyzed the data
The data covers race results, odds, lap times and more from 1986 to July 2021. It is very large — too large to open fully in Excel. That is exactly why you need to decide where to look.
Download the data with your own account. Do not give it to others or publish it on the internet.
